summary: Roaming between APs causes corporate VPN to stay bound to stale interface; internal connections fail until client restart
summary_detail: Multiple engineers reported that after walking between floors or moving across AP groups, their Redwood corporate VPN client continued to route via the old (disconnected) virtual interface. Internal traffic (SSH, gRPC to internal clusters) stalled with TCP RSTs or timeouts until the VPN client was restarted or routes were manually flushed.
impact: Intermittent loss of connectivity to internal services for engineers on corporate Wi-Fi while on the corporate VPN. Blocks developer workflows, remote debugging, and can cause failed job submissions. Affects both macOS and Windows users but more frequent on Windows 10/11 with aggressive roaming enabled.
environment_detail: Corp Wi-Fi: WPA2-Enterprise with 802.11k/r enabled on Aruba APs, DHCP via internal DHCP clusters; VPN: corporate WireGuard-based client (rw-vpn), version 1.2.3 on Windows and 1.2.1 on macOS. Observed mostly in us-east office floors where AP density and roaming handoffs occur frequently.
steps_to_reproduce: Connect laptop to corporate Wi-Fi on floor A and establish rw-vpn connection to internal gateway
SSH into an internal jump host or maintain an active gRPC stream to a dev service
Walk (or force roaming) to an adjacent AP on floor B causing Wi-Fi reassociation
Observe that VPN client reports connection still active but internal traffic stalls
Restart rw-vpn client or run 'sudo ip route flush' / 'wg-quick down && wg-quick up' to restore connectivity
observed_behavior: Existing TCP sessions to internal hosts either hang (no packets forwarded) or receive immediate RSTs. System network stack shows old tun/tap interface still present with routes pointing to a previous gateway. The VPN client logs show no clear disconnect event and does not auto-rebind to the new underlying physical interface.
expected_behavior: On underlying network interface change (Wi-Fi reassociation), VPN client should detect link change, rebind/tunnel across the new adapter, and preserve or gracefully re-establish active sessions where possible.
logs_and_traces: Windows 10 client netstat: stale route via "rw-vpn0" and no outbound packets after roam (logs attached to ticket)
WireGuard debug: no handshake errors logged; last handshake timestamp unchanged despite change of physical interface
tcpdump on client NIC: reassociation to new AP followed by ARP retries; VPN encapsulated traffic stops after roaming
Core router logs: no apparent drop on VPN gateway side; peer remains active
investigation_notes: Hypothesis 1: VPN client does not subscribe to OS netlink events on Windows, so it misses interface index changes and keeps binding socket to old interface handle.
Hypothesis 2: Quick roaming causes a short DHCP renewal and interface index remap which leaves existing tun/tap bindings invalid until process restart.
Reproduced locally: Sophie reproduced on Windows 11 with a scripted AP switch; verified that restarting the VPN client restores proper routes immediately.
Checked AP configuration: 802.11k/r enabled and transition thresholds set to aggressive values. DHCP lease times are short in the affected VLAN (60s) which may accelerate rebinding issues.
No server-side rate limiting or gateway termination observed; peer remains listed in WireGuard peers table at the gateway during failures.
Related prior internal tickets checked: none match this exact symptom; see linked runbook for VPN client restart procedure.
workaround: In the short term, users should restart the rw-vpn client after roaming or run the provided PowerShell script (attached) to flush stale routes and reinitialize the tunnel. IT can also ask users to disable aggressive fast-roaming in Wi-Fi adapter properties as a temporary mitigation.
proposed_fix: Engineering to update rw-vpn client to handle interface change events (netlink on Linux/macOS, Windows Network List Manager or RegisterNetworkChangeNotification on Windows) and rebind sockets dynamically. Also add an optional 'rebind-on-network-change' flag to the client config.
resolution_timeline: Investigation started 2026-03-12. Engineering prioritization discussion scheduled 2026-03-13. Short-term mitigation (doc + PowerShell) published same day. Long-term client fix targeted for 1.3.x release in April 2026.
